title: The Didache's prayer (Didache 9)
hook: as this bread was scattered on the hills and gathered into one
tomorrow: why would a man beg his friends not to rescue him?

segments.voice: Catherine's book closed for us on tears, climbing from fear to love, with fire for those who can't cry. The line was tears of love.
screen: `TEARS OF LOVE.` → `THE EARLY CHURCH, IN ITS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: A potluck table: tamales from one kitchen, rice from another, somebody's grandmother's cake. An hour ago this meal was scattered across a whole town. Now it's one table. An old Christian handbook called the Didache has a prayer built on that same picture, only smaller: one loaf, and the grain it came from.
screen: `A POTLUCK TABLE.` → `SCATTERED ACROSS A TOWN.` → `NOW ONE MEAL.`

segments.voice: Didache is Greek for teaching, and chapter nine is a thanksgiving over a cup and over broken bread. It thanks the Father for the life and knowledge made known through Jesus, his servant. Then the picture. As this broken bread was scattered over the hills and, gathered together, became one, so may your Church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom. Grain from many hillsides; one loaf; people from everywhere, one Church. And it's honest about limits: the same chapter says only the baptized should eat and drink of this Eucharist. Giving thanks over bread is something a neighbor tradition knows in its own words. In the Mishnah, a foundational book of Jewish law, the blessing over bread praises God who brings forth bread from the earth. Jews call it the hamotzi, and families say it over challah on Shabbat. Some scholars hear Jewish meal blessings in the Didache's thanksgivings. Here's what's shared: before eating, both name God as the giver of bread. Here's the honest difference. The hamotzi is said over bread at any meal, thanking God for what the earth brings forth. The Didache's prayer is said over the bread of the Eucharist, gives thanks through Jesus, and asks for one thing more: that the scattered be gathered.
screen: `THANKS OVER BROKEN BREAD.` · `SCATTERED ON THE HILLS, MADE ONE.` · `WHO BRINGS FORTH BREAD FROM THE EARTH.` · `SHARED THANKS, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `GATHERED INTO ONE.`

segments.voice: If there's bread or a cracker nearby, hold a small piece before eating it, and think of how many fields and hands it came from, scattered, now one piece in your palm; then eat it slowly. With nothing nearby, hold an open hand and think of one meal that gathered people from different places. Those who pray can ask, as the Didache does, that the Church be gathered into one.
The Didache's prayer. Thanks over broken bread, and a plea that the Church be gathered from the ends of the earth.
Carry this: gathered into one, the way grain from many hills becomes a loaf. Sleep well.

chat.says: banquet: Hannah said a Hebrew blessing over her challah. Mia asked if it's like our grace. is it?
options: Alike in thanking God for bread before eating. Different words and setting: hers is for any meal.
Exactly the same prayer. Every religion's grace is one blessing in different languages.
Not alike. Hers is about food rules and ours is about thanks, so they can't overlap.
chat.meaning: Jews bless God who brings forth bread from the earth; the Didache gives thanks over the Eucharist's bread through Jesus. Shared thanks, honest difference.

Didache.meaning: an old Christian handbook; its name is Greek for teaching

Eucharist.meaning: the sacrament of Christ's body and blood, received at Mass

Mishnah.meaning: a foundational collection of Jewish law and teaching

hamotzi.meaning: the Jewish blessing over bread: who brings forth bread from the earth

challah.meaning: braided bread blessed in Jewish homes on Shabbat

Shabbat.meaning: the Jewish Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening

sources.work: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)

notes: Didache 9 paraphrased (not quoted): thanksgiving over the cup ('the holy vine of David thy servant') and the broken bread ('the life and knowledge which thou didst make known unto us through Jesus thy Servant'); 'as this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains and being gathered together became one, so may thy Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into thy kingdom'; none may eat or drink of the eucharist but the baptized. A Keeper may choose to quote Lightfoot exactly.
'Didache is Greek for teaching': the Greek word means teaching, and the work's title calls it a teaching; no date is given for the text. Confirm.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Mishnah Berakhot 6:1 paraphrased: over bread one says 'who brings forth bread from the earth' (ha-motzi lechem min ha-aretz). 'Families say it over challah on Shabbat' is descriptive; confirm with a Jewish scholar. 'Some scholars hear Jewish meal blessings in the Didache's thanksgivings' is hedged; confirm. The shared thing (thanks to God over bread before eating) and the honest difference (any meal vs. the Eucharist, through Jesus, with a plea for gathering) are stated without ranking; never 'the same prayer'.
The fork's wrong option 'come to Mass and receive the Eucharist with us' reflects the honest limit in Didache 9 and Catholic practice (Communion for the baptized in full communion); confirm wording.
